title: Acoustic Phenomena — 24 MCQs
description: Covers sound waves and pressure amplitude, intensity, loudness, quality, pitch, and Doppler’s effect with conceptual and numerical questions.

questions.q: What is pressure amplitude in a sound wave?
options: The maximum variation in pressure from the equilibrium pressure
The average pressure of the medium
The maximum displacement of particles from their mean positions
The rate of transfer of sound energy per unit area
questions.explanation: Pressure amplitude is the maximum change in pressure above or below the equilibrium pressure of the medium as a sound wave passes.

questions.q: Which of the following is the SI unit of pressure amplitude?
questions.explanation: Pressure amplitude is a pressure quantity, so its SI unit is the pascal (Pa).

questions.q: The intensity of a sound wave in a given medium is proportional to which quantity squared?
options: Pressure amplitude and particle displacement amplitude independently
questions.explanation: For a sinusoidal sound wave in a given medium, intensity is proportional to the square of pressure amplitude: I ∝ (Δpₘₐₓ)².

questions.q: If the pressure amplitude of a sound wave is doubled while the frequency and medium remain unchanged, its intensity becomes
questions.explanation: Since intensity is proportional to the square of pressure amplitude, I₂/I₁ = (2Δp₁/Δp₁)² = 4.

questions.q: Which physical quantity is most directly associated with the perception of how loud a sound is?
questions.explanation: Loudness is the subjective perception of sound strength and is related to sound intensity, although it also depends on frequency and the sensitivity of the human ear.

questions.q: The intensity of a sound wave is 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻². If the threshold intensity of hearing is 1.0 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻², what is the sound intensity level?
questions.explanation: The intensity level is β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) = 10 log₁₀(10⁻⁶/10⁻¹²) = 10 × 6 = 60 dB.

questions.q: Two sounds have intensities in the ratio 100:1. What is the difference in their intensity levels?
questions.explanation: The difference is Δβ = 10 log₁₀(I₁/I₂) = 10 log₁₀(100) = 20 dB.

questions.q: Which characteristic of sound enables us to distinguish between a flute and a violin playing the same note at the same loudness?
questions.explanation: Quality, or timbre, distinguishes sounds from different sources even when their fundamental frequencies and intensities are the same. It depends mainly on the waveform and its harmonic content.

questions.q: The pitch of a sound is primarily determined by its
questions.explanation: Pitch is the auditory sensation associated primarily with frequency. A higher frequency is generally perceived as a higher-pitched sound.

questions.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and travels at 340 m s⁻¹. What is its wavelength?

A sound wave has a pressure amplitude of 2.0 Pa. If its pressure amplitude increases to 6.0 Pa in the same medium at the same frequency, what is the ratio of the new intensity to the original intensity?
questions.explanation: Since I ∝ (Δp)², I₂/I₁ = (6/2)² = 9. The intensity ratio is therefore 9:1.

questions.q: What is the Doppler effect?
options: The absorption of sound by a material
The conversion of sound energy into heat
The change in sound intensity caused only by increasing amplitude
The apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between a source and an observer
questions.explanation: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in observed frequency caused by relative motion between the source and the observer.

questions.q: A source of sound approaches a stationary observer. What happens to the observed frequency?
questions.explanation: As the source approaches, successive wavefronts reach the observer more frequently, so the observed frequency increases.

questions.q: A source emitting sound at 500 Hz approaches a stationary observer at 20 m s⁻¹. If the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, what frequency does the observer hear?
questions.explanation: For an approaching source and a stationary observer, f′ = fv/(v − vₛ) = 500 × 340/(340 − 20) = 170000/320 ≈ 531 Hz.

questions.q: A stationary source emits a sound of frequency 600 Hz. An observer moves toward the source at 10 m s⁻¹. If the speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹, what is the observed frequency?
questions.explanation: For an observer approaching a stationary source, f′ = f(v + vₒ)/v = 600 × (330 + 10)/330 ≈ 618 Hz.

questions.q: A source emitting sound at 800 Hz moves away from a stationary observer at 40 m s⁻¹. If the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, what is the observed frequency?
questions.explanation: For a source moving away from a stationary observer, f′ = fv/(v + vₛ) = 800 × 340/(340 + 40) = 272000/380 ≈ 716 Hz. The closest option is 715 Hz.

questions.q: A train approaches a stationary observer while sounding its whistle. Which expression gives the observed frequency if f is the emitted frequency, v is the speed of sound, and vₛ is the source speed toward the observer?
questions.explanation: For a source approaching a stationary observer, the wavefronts are compressed and the observed frequency is f′ = fv/(v − vₛ).

questions.q: A stationary observer hears a 1000 Hz siren from a source moving away at 30 m s⁻¹. If the speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹, what is the observed frequency?
When a sound source and an observer move toward each other through a stationary medium, the observed frequency is
options: Always equal to the emitted frequency
Always less than the emitted frequency
questions.explanation: When both source and observer approach each other, the observer encounters wavefronts more frequently. The observed frequency is therefore higher than the emitted frequency.

questions.q: A source and an observer are at rest relative to each other in a stationary medium. Which statement about the Doppler effect is correct?
options: The observed frequency must be greater than the emitted frequency
The observed frequency must be lower than the emitted frequency
The observed frequency depends only on the sound amplitude
The observed frequency equals the emitted frequency
questions.explanation: With no relative motion between the source and observer, there is no Doppler frequency shift, so f′ = f.

questions.q: A sound wave has an intensity of 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻². What is its intensity level relative to the threshold intensity of 1.0 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻²?
questions.explanation: β = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) = 10 log₁₀(4.0 × 10⁸) = 10(8 + log₁₀4) ≈ 86 dB.

questions.q: For a plane sinusoidal sound wave in a medium of density ρ and sound speed v, what is the average intensity in terms of pressure amplitude Δpₘₐₓ?
questions.explanation: For a plane sinusoidal sound wave, the pressure amplitude and particle displacement are related through the medium's acoustic properties. The average intensity is I = (Δpₘₐₓ)²/(2ρv).

questions.q: A source of sound of frequency 400 Hz moves toward a stationary observer at 20 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the increase in the observed frequency?
questions.explanation: The observed frequency is f′ = 400 × 340/(340 − 20) = 136000/320 = 425 Hz. The increase is 425 − 400 = 25 Hz, so option C is correct.
